newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Cadbury shares rise, outlook good.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Cadbury shares rise, outlook good.

text.p: British soft drinks to chocolate group Cadbury Schweppes Plc posted a two percent increase in its half year profits to 236 million pounds ($383.4 million) on Wednesday, with chief executive John Sunderland saying the group had made a good start to its second half.

"It's very early obviously, but we have had a fairly encouraging start and we also get a pretty clear picture about Christmas now because most of the major Christmas orders are already taken. So we feel confident about the outcome of our seasonal Christmas business," he told Reuters in an interview.
The company makes about 60 percent of its profits in the second half of the year as confectionery sales surge in winter and at Christmas.
Cadbury shares were 16p higher at 611p as brokers responded favourably to a set of figures above most stockmarket forecasts.
Trading profits from its beverages division rose by 29 percent to 198 million pounds in the six months to June 14 while the confectionery division achieved a three percent rise to 105 million.
The strength of sterling on foreign exchange markets however reduced earnings from the beverages division by 11 million pounds and by five million for the confectionery division.
The company's results were released overnight on the Australian Stock Exchange, where it is also listed, by its local offshoot, Cadbury Schweppes Australia Ltd.
Turnover from continuing operations fell to 1.837 billion pounds from 1.894 billion, a rise of five percent on a constant currency basis.

Cadbury, which sold its 51 percent stake in Coca-Cola Schweppes Beverages Ltd (CCSB) in June for 623 million pounds, now had more room for acquisitions, said Sunderland. The sale of the group's CCSB interest cut borrowings by 45 percent to 882 million at the half-year stage and led to a pre-tax gain of 417 million.
Sunderland said he expected the group to make two or three acquisitions in the confectionery area in the next year for between 100 and 200 million pounds each.

"The opportunities are more in confectionery than beverages because the end game in beverages is far more played out in terms of consolidation. The top three guys have over 80 percent in beverages whereas in confectionery the top six have less than 50," said Sunderland.

"Yes I think you can expect to see the pattern we have had in previous years of one or two acquisitions in confectionery continuing. They are mid range acquisitions of between about 100 and 200 million and mainly of the infill type," he said.

In North America, where there have been worries over the ability of Cadbury's subsidiary Dr Pepper/7UP to compete with the might of Coca-Cola and PepsiCo colas, Sunderland said the group has managed to slow the rate of sales decline of soft drink 7UP.
"We have slowed the rate of decline. It was going down by about four percent per annum pretty steadily and we have bought that back to two and the trend is actually stabilising.
"The core 7UP brand has actually grown. We have chosen to support the key brand and that is paying off gradually, but I don't want to be over optimistic," said Sunderland.

In the six months, Dr Pepper sales rose 4.3 percent, out growing overall soft drinks market growth of three percent. The United States accounts for about 40 percent of soft drinks sold world-wide. Some 60 percent of soft drinks consumed in the Americas are colas.
Beverage sales in the United States make up some 60 percent of Cadbury-Schweppes total drinks sales and drink sales alone in the region contribute about 35 percent of total group profits.

Sunderland said the group planned to spend slightly more than 350 million pounds on marketing in the second half, with the launch of a national television campaign in Britain for a new biscuit snack called Astros. ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
